new.title: Tell the time on the Rheinturm
new.desc: Düsseldorf's 240 metre TV tower doubles as the world's biggest decimal clock: the round lights running up its shaft, the Lichtzeitpegel, show hours, minutes and seconds.
new.tip: Read it from top to bottom in three groups (hours, minutes, seconds) from the Rhine meadows in Oberkassel, then ride up at dusk for a drink while the city lights come on.

new.title: Watch the Gehry buildings bend at sunset
new.desc: The three crooked towers of the Neuer Zollhof, Frank Gehry's 1999 trio of white plaster, brick and mirror steel, turned an old customs harbour into the city's favourite photo spot.
new.tip: Come in the last hour of daylight, when the skyscrapers of the Medienhafen reflect in the water; the footbridge across the harbour basin gives the best angle.

new.title: Spot the twisted spire of St. Lambertus
new.desc: The brick Gothic basilica on the Stiftsplatz is the Altstadt's landmark, and its spire visibly corkscrews, a warp locals love to explain with their own legends.
new.tip: Walk round to quiet Liefergasse beside the church for an ornate old house front few visitors notice.

new.title: Hunt for Radschläger, the cartwheeling kids
new.desc: Cartwheeling children are Düsseldorf's oldest tradition, said to date back to the victory at Worringen in 1288. The 1954 Radschlägerbrunnen on the Burgplatz honours them under old plane trees.
new.tip: Once you have seen the fountain, look down: the little cartwheeler also decorates manhole covers around the city, and there is another figure by the Uerige brewery.

new.title: Check the Rhine's mood at the Pegeluhr
new.desc: This riverside clock on the promenade tells you not only the time but also the current water level of the Rhine, a number Düsseldorfers watch closely when floods or droughts make the news.
new.tip: Compare the reading with the flood marks on the Altstadt walls nearby to see how high the river has risen in the past.

new.title: Read the city's birth story in bronze
new.desc: Bert Gerresheim's Stadterhebungsmonument packs the founding of Düsseldorf into one tall sculpture, from the Battle of Worringen in 1288 to the granting of town rights.
new.tip: Walk all the way around it: the scenes and faces, including the city's founders, only make sense from different sides.

new.title: Pose in front of Sarah Morris's tiled wall
new.desc: Behind the K20 museum, artist Sarah Morris covered 180 square metres of wall with glossy geometric tiles, an artwork locals use as a backdrop for photos.
new.tip: Combine it with a look into K20 next door, which holds the state's collection of twentieth century art, from Klee to Warhol.

new.title: Walk the painted houses of Kiefernstraße
new.desc: In Flingern-Süd, a whole row of former squats on Kiefernstraße is painted from pavement to roof, a living open-air gallery and one of the city's alternative strongholds.
new.tip: Be respectful, people live here. Afterwards, browse the indie shops and cafés of Flingern on Ackerstraße.

new.title: Climb the Kaiserpfalz ruins in Kaiserswerth
new.desc: On the Rhine at the northern tip of the city lie the ruins of an imperial palace that grew from a monastery founded around 700, next to a village of baroque houses and cobbled lanes.
new.tip: Cycle here along the Rhine (about an hour from the Altstadt) or take the boat, then have an ice cream or a beer in the garden of the Burghof by the ruins.

new.title: Stroll the gardens of pink Schloss Benrath
new.desc: Built in the 1750s and 60s for Elector Carl Theodor, Benrath's rococo pleasure palace is locals' 'pink castle', with long canals and a huge park in the far south of the city.
new.tip: The park is free; come on a summer evening when the light turns the façade rosy, and book a guided tour if you want to see the domed hall inside.

new.title: Find calm in the Japanese garden of the Nordpark
new.desc: A gift from the city's Japanese community, this 5,000 square metre garden with ponds, stone lanterns and pruned pines sits inside the big Nordpark.
new.tip: Go on a weekday morning for near silence; it is free, and the U78 stops close by.

new.title: Visit a Buddhist temple in Niederkassel
new.desc: The EKO-Haus der Japanischen Kultur is a real Jodo Shinshu temple with a Japanese garden and a traditional house, built for the largest Japanese community in Germany.
new.tip: Check the programme before you go: the temple opens on set days, and tea ceremonies and festivals are the best way to see it in use.

new.title: Travel 8,000 years in clay at the Hetjens
new.desc: Germany's ceramics museum, in the baroque Palais Nesselrode, holds pots, tiles and porcelain up to 8,000 years old from every corner of the world.
new.tip: The Filmmuseum shares the same address, so you can pair the two on a rainy afternoon.

new.title: Go underground for art at KIT
new.desc: Kunst im Tunnel is a gallery squeezed into a leftover tunnel space two metres beneath the Rhine promenade, showing young artists, many from the city's famous academy.
new.tip: Look for the glass pavilion on the promenade near the Rheinkniebrücke; the café on top is a pleasant stop by the river.

new.title: People-watch along the Kö-Graben
new.desc: The Königsallee is Düsseldorf's luxury boulevard, split by a tree-lined moat with the Tritonenbrunnen at its end: one bank for designer shops, the other for banks and cafés.
new.tip: Grab a seat outside a café on the Kö and watch the style parade; the moat bridges are the classic photo spot.

new.title: Climb the last castle tower on the Burgplatz
new.desc: The Schlossturm is all that is left of the ducal palace, and it now houses a small museum on 2,000 years of Rhine shipping.
new.tip: Save time for Café Laterne at the top, with a fine view over the river and the Altstadt roofs.

new.title: Drink an Uerige standing on the street
new.desc: The Uerige on Berger Straße has brewed its bitter, hoppy Altbier since 1862, and on warm evenings the crowd spills out until drinkers stand all the way across Rheinstraße.
new.tip: Do as the locals: stand at a barrel outside and let the Köbes (waiter) swap your empty glass for a full one until you put your beer mat on top.

new.title: Order Sauerbraten at Im Füchschen
new.desc: One of only four traditional Altbier house breweries left, the wood-panelled Füchschen on Ratinger Straße pours a mellower Alt than its rivals and serves solid Rhineland cooking.
new.tip: Try the Rheinischer Sauerbraten; afterwards stay on Ratinger Straße, the Altstadt's favourite street among locals.
new.q: Brauerei Im Füchschen Ratinger Straße Düsseldorf

new.title: Raise a Schlüssel Alt by the Neanderkirche
new.desc: The smallest of the four classic house breweries has brewed Schlüssel Alt on Bolkerstraße since 1850, and it uses the churchyard of the baroque Neanderkirche as its beer garden.
new.tip: Have your first glass in the church beer garden, then peek into the Neanderkirche to see its organ.

new.title: Taste Altbier at its source in the Schumacher
new.desc: Brauerei Schumacher on Oststraße is the oldest Altbier brewery still going, pouring its smooth Schumacher Alt in the original brewhouse since 1838.
new.tip: It is outside the Altstadt crush, so it is a good pick for a quieter dinner; watch the Köbes keep tally with pencil strokes on your beer mat.

new.title: Start the night at Brauerei Kürzer
new.desc: The newcomer among the Altstadt brewpubs serves a darker Alt to a young crowd on Kurze Straße, and locals use it as the warm-up before the bars and dance floors.
new.tip: Go early on a Friday or Saturday: by ten it is packed.

new.title: Knock back a Killepitsch through the window
new.desc: This red herbal liqueur was first poured in 1955 at Et Kabüffke, a tiny tasting room in Flinger Straße opposite the Uerige; locals swear by it as a digestif.
new.tip: You do not need to go in: order a shot through the little window onto the street, and buy a bottle as a souvenir next door.

new.title: Taste Düsseldorf Mostert at the Löwensenf shop
new.desc: Düsseldorf is a mustard town, and Löwensenf has made its sharp mustard here since the 1920s. Its Altstadt shop lets you taste a whole row of varieties.
new.tip: For the oldest local brand, ABB Mostert in a stoneware pot, head to the spice shop Gewürzhaus Vogel nearby.

new.title: Graze through the Carlsplatz market
new.desc: The oldest market square still in use in Düsseldorf is a daily covered food market of cheese, wine, olive oil, fresh produce and snack stalls in the Carlstadt.
new.tip: Come for a late breakfast or lunch on a weekday and save room for a tart from Pure Pastry.

new.title: Queue for ramen on Immermannstraße
new.desc: Around Immermannstraße lies Little Tokyo, home to one of Europe's largest Japanese communities, and its ramen bars are a local obsession; Takumi is the most famous.
new.tip: Arrive before noon or after two: between twelve and one the line stretches down the pavement.

new.title: Slurp handmade soba at Soba-an
new.desc: In Little Tokyo, Soba-an makes its buckwheat noodles by hand, a rarity in Europe; National Geographic credits it to Japan's only female soba master.
new.tip: Order the cold soba with dipping sauce to taste the noodles at their best.

new.title: Join the queue at Bäckerei Hinkel
new.desc: This family bakery has been baking since 1891, and Düsseldorfers queue for its bread, fruit tarts and almond croissants.
new.tip: Do not let the line scare you; it moves fast, and staff sometimes hand out samples outside.

new.title: Drink Gulasch Alt in Oberkassel's old station
new.desc: On the left bank, the Brauerei Alter Bahnhof fills a former station building on Belsenplatz and brews its own Gulasch Alt, a neighbourhood local far from the tourist crowds.
new.tip: Combine it with a walk along Luegallee and the Art Nouveau villas of Oberkassel.

new.title: Wake the Hoppeditz at 11:11 on 11 November
new.desc: Carnival season begins when the jester Hoppeditz climbs out of his mustard pot in front of the Rathaus and gives the city a mocking 'Narrenschelte'.
new.tip: Get to the Marktplatz well before eleven in costume; the party moves into the Altstadt pubs right afterwards.

new.title: Dress up for the Kö-Treiben
new.desc: On carnival Sunday the Königsallee turns into an informal street party, with the city's most elaborate costumes and small homemade floats.
new.tip: This is the day to show off a costume; bring small change for the street kiosks and a warm layer.

new.title: Catch the satire floats on Rosenmontag
new.desc: Düsseldorf's Rose Monday parade is famous across Europe for Jacques Tilly's biting political floats, which regularly make international headlines.
new.tip: Stand along Heinrich-Heine-Allee and shout 'Helau' (never 'Alaaf', that is Cologne) to catch sweets and flowers.

new.title: Watch the sunset from the Rhine steps
new.desc: The wide steps down to the river at the Burgplatz are where Düsseldorf gathers on summer evenings, with street musicians and the sun dropping behind Oberkassel.
new.tip: Do like the locals and pick up a cold beer from a Büdchen (corner kiosk) on the way.

new.title: Grab a deck chair at the Stadtstrand
new.desc: In summer, sand, deck chairs and a bar pop up beside the Rhine bridges, with bratwurst, cold drinks and a full view of the river.
new.tip: The spot by the Oberkasseler Brücke has free live music; check the programme on their Instagram.

new.title: Ride the Ferris wheel at the Rheinkirmes
new.desc: For ten days every July, around four million people flock to the Oberkassel riverside for one of Germany's biggest funfairs, with the Altstadt skyline across the water.
new.tip: Come for the Friday fireworks over the Rhine and watch them from the Altstadt bank if the fair is too crowded.

new.title: Crawl through the net of 'in orbit' at K21
new.desc: Tomás Saraceno's installation hangs steel nets more than 25 metres above the glass dome hall of the Ständehaus, and you can climb onto them and look straight down.
new.tip: Wear shoes with grip and do not go on a full stomach; the museum hands out overalls.

new.title: Rummage at the Aachener Platz flea market
new.desc: Every Saturday hundreds of dealers spread out on the Aachener Platz in Bilk, one of the region's largest flea markets, where up to 20,000 people hunt for bargains.
new.tip: Arrive early for the best finds, then warm up with weekend jazz at Café Sperrmüll on site.

new.title: Feed the deer in the Grafenberg Wildpark
new.desc: One of Germany's oldest game parks lies in a 200-year-old beech forest on the eastern edge of town, home to deer, wild boar and other native animals.
new.tip: Entry is free; pack carrots or apples cut into pieces and follow the forest paths on to the 'Schöne Aussicht' viewpoint.

new.title: Swim or paddle at the Unterbacher See
new.desc: On the city's eastern edge, this lake is Düsseldorf's summer playground, with lidos on the north and south beaches and boards and sails for hire.
new.tip: The south side has a surf and kite school; jog or cycle the lap around the lake if the weather is not warm enough to swim.

new.title: Take the free tour of the old Rathaus
new.desc: Düsseldorf's Renaissance town hall on the Marktplatz dates from 1570, and on Wednesdays the city opens its halls on a free guided walk.
new.tip: Meet in the foyer in the afternoon; in front of the building, check out the Jan Wellem horseman and the little statue of the boy who saved its casting.

new.title: Take an espresso into the Hofgarten
new.desc: Germany's oldest public park stretches from the Kö to the Rhine, with trees up to 200 years old, ponds and quiet lawns right next to the busy centre.
new.tip: Pick up a coffee at Pocchino on the park side of the Kö, then stroll to Schloss Jägerhof at the far end.

new.title: Look up at the Müngstener Brücke
new.desc: Opened in 1897 between Solingen and Remscheid, Germany's highest railway bridge spans the Wupper valley 107 metres up on an elegant steel arch.
new.tip: Walk down into the Brückenpark beneath it for the best view and time your visit for a train rumbling across.

new.title: Storm Schloss Burg above the Wupper
new.desc: The rebuilt twelfth century castle of the Counts of Berg in Solingen-Burg is the region's showpiece, with the Bergisches Museum, a knights' hall and wide views over the wooded valley.
new.tip: Park or get off the bus in Unterburg and walk up through the old village; the views on the way make up for the climb.

new.title: Wander the Skulpturenpark Waldfrieden in Wuppertal
new.desc: Sculptor Tony Cragg turned a forest estate in Wuppertal into an open-air museum where his own works and those of other artists stand among the trees and in glass pavilions.
new.tip: Look out for the mirror pieces, and end with coffee and cake at Café Podest on the grounds.

new.title: Climb the rainbow Holsteiner Treppe in Wuppertal
new.desc: Hilly Wuppertal has hundreds of public staircases; on this one, artist Horst Gläsker painted each of the 112 steps a different colour and added words like 'Liebe' and 'Wut' that you only read going up.
new.tip: Climb it, do not descend it, or you will miss the words; residents repaint it themselves when it fades.

new.title: Explore Hollein's Museum Abteiberg in Mönchengladbach
new.desc: Hans Hollein's 1982 museum is an icon of postmodern architecture, stepping down the abbey hill beside the Münster and filled with Beuys, Richter, Warhol and other modern art.
new.tip: Do not skip the terraced sculpture garden on the old abbey slope; the Alter Markt with its cafés is a minute away.

new.title: Get lost on the Museum Insel Hombroich
new.desc: Near Neuss, Erwin Heerich's brick pavilions are scattered through a wild meadow and riverside landscape on the Erft, with art shown without any labels, just as the founder wanted.
new.tip: Allow half a day; take the S-Bahn to Neuss Süd and the bus from there, and stop at the cafeteria building for a simple lunch.

new.title: See Tadao Ando's bunker of glass at the Langen Foundation
new.desc: On a former NATO missile base outside Neuss, Tadao Ando built a concrete and glass gallery half sunk into earth walls, for a collection of modern and Japanese art.
new.tip: It is a short walk from Insel Hombroich, so pair the two; the approach through the earth wall is part of the experience.

new.title: Walk the walls of the toll fortress of Zons
new.desc: In 1372 the archbishops of Cologne moved their Rhine toll to Zons, and the little fortified town in Dormagen still has its walls, towers and a windmill on the ramparts.
new.tip: Arrive from Düsseldorf-Urdenbach on the Rhine car ferry, and check the open-air stage for its summer fairy-tale plays.

new.title: See right through it at the Röntgen-Museum in Lennep
new.desc: Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen, discoverer of X-rays, was born in Remscheid-Lennep, and the German Röntgen Museum tells his story with hands-on science.
new.tip: Afterwards walk the slate-clad old town of Lennep, where Röntgen's birthplace still stands.

new.title: Stand on Germany's westernmost point in Selfkant
new.desc: Near Isenbruch, the westernmost village in Germany, a memorial stone marks the country's westernmost point on land, with the Netherlands just across the fields.
new.tip: The stone stands by road K 1 near Haus Groevenkamp; it makes a nice stop on a bike ride through the flat Selfkant.

new.title: Sharpen up at the Klingenmuseum in Gräfrath
new.desc: Solingen is Germany's blade city, and its museum in a former convent in Gräfrath claims the world's largest cutlery collection, along with swords and the story of local smiths.
new.tip: Leave time for the cobbled Gräfrath market square below the museum, the prettiest corner of Solingen.

new.title: Dunk a Burger Brezel in Solingen-Burg
new.desc: Not a lye pretzel at all, the Burger Brezel is a sweet, dry pastry made in Burg since about 1795, hand-knotted and listed in Slow Food's Ark of Taste.
new.tip: Dip it in coffee ('zoppen', as locals say), and buy one on a ribbon to wear home round your neck.

new.title: Sit down to a Bergische Kaffeetafel at Schloss Burg
new.desc: The region's festive coffee spread brings waffles, rice pudding, raisin bread, black bread, apple butter and more, with coffee poured from a tapped pot called the Dröppelminna.
new.tip: It is a full meal, so skip lunch; the castle restaurant serves it, often with hot cherries.

new.title: Drink Wupper Hell in a former swimming pool
new.desc: The Wuppertaler Brauhaus in Barmen brews its own beers inside a nineteenth century public bath, with the tanks set where swimmers once did their lengths.
new.tip: Order the house Wupper Hell or Dunkel with something hearty; there is often live music at night.

new.title: Have a coffee at Utopiastadt's Hutmacher
new.desc: The old Mirker Bahnhof in Wuppertal is now Utopiastadt, a creative hub with workshops, a community garden and the café Hutmacher, right on the Nordbahntrasse.
new.tip: Borrow one of the free bikes here and ride the old railway line; check for concerts and exhibitions in the evening.

new.title: Toast the view at the Hardt-Terrassen
new.desc: Wuppertal's oldest beer garden sits next to the red brick Elisenturm in the Hardt, Germany's oldest park created by citizens, high above Elberfeld.
new.tip: Climb the Elisenturm first, then pop into the free botanical garden greenhouses next door.

new.title: Linger at Katzengold in the Luisenviertel
new.desc: Wuppertal's Luisenviertel is a lively old-town quarter of small shops and cafés, and Katzengold is one of its best-known hangouts.
new.tip: Afterwards climb the steps up to the Ölberg, the old workers' hill behind the quarter.

new.title: Eat cake in Neuss's oldest timber-framed house
new.desc: Kaffeehaus 1571 in Neuss serves homemade cakes and coffee inside the city's oldest half-timbered house, a short walk from the Quirinus-Münster.
new.tip: Pair it with a look into the late Romanesque Quirinus-Münster and the Obertor, the last of Neuss's medieval gates.

new.title: Ride the Wuppertal Schwebebahn end to end
new.desc: Since 1901 Wuppertal's suspension railway has hung upside down over the Wupper river, swaying past 20 stations over 13 kilometres, still part of everyday transport.
new.tip: Sit at the very front or back for the view; a round trip from Vohwinkel to Oberbarmen takes about an hour.

new.title: Cycle the Nordbahntrasse to the Lego bridge
new.desc: An old railway line through Wuppertal is now a cycling and walking path through tunnels and over viaducts, and one bridge was painted by street artist MEGX to look like giant Lego bricks.
new.tip: Get off and look at the bridge from Schwesterstraße below for the full effect.

new.title: Meet your ancestors in the Neandertal
new.desc: The museum near Mettmann stands close to the spot where the first Neanderthal was found in 1856, and tells the story of humanity with hands-on exhibits.
new.tip: Try the morphing station that turns you into a Neanderthal; bus 741 stops right outside from Düsseldorf or Mettmann.

new.title: Birdwatch at the Krickenbecker Seen
new.desc: Four lakes near Nettetal, dug out by peat cutting centuries ago and protected since 1938, draw goosanders, smew and flocks of ducks in winter.
new.tip: Park at the information centre and follow the wide paved path between the lakes; bring binoculars.

new.title: Watch the parade at the Neusser Bürger-Schützenfest
new.desc: On the last weekend of August, Neuss throws one of the world's biggest marksmen's festivals, with thousands of uniformed members marching through town and up to a million visitors.
new.tip: Find a spot near the Markt for the big parade and stay for the fair.

new.title: Pull yourself across on the Müngsten Schwebefähre
new.desc: In the Brückenpark below the Müngstener Brücke, a hand-powered suspension ferry lets you crank yourself across the Wupper.
new.tip: Come on a dry weekend afternoon; from the park, trails lead along the river towards Burg.

new.title: Hike round the Eschbachtalsperre in Remscheid
new.desc: Finished in 1891, this was Germany's first dam built for drinking water, and today a wooded loop path runs around the reservoir.
new.tip: Combine it with a walk in the valley down to the old hammer mills of Remscheid.
